title: Operating Systems
overview: System software makes the hardware usable. Paper 1 asks why a computer needs an operating system, what the OS does in each of its management roles (memory, files, security, hardware and processes), what common utility programs are for, and why programmers use library programs, including dynamic link libraries (DLLs). Answers score when each task is linked to a specific action the OS or utility performs.
syllabusPoints: Explain why a computer system requires an operating system.

Explain the key management tasks carried out by the operating system, including memory management, file management, security management, hardware management (input/output/peripherals) and process management.

Show understanding of the need for typical utility software, including disk formatter, virus checker, defragmentation software, disk contents analysis/disk repair software, file compression and back-up software.
Show understanding that software under development is often constructed using existing code from program libraries.
Describe the benefits to the developer of software constructed using library files, including dynamic link library (DLL) files.

definitions.definition: System software that manages the computer's hardware and software resources and provides an interface between the user, applications and the hardware.
System software that performs a specific maintenance or management task, such as backing up, compressing or checking for malware.
A program that has been loaded into memory and is being executed.
Software that lets the operating system communicate with a particular hardware device.
When a file is stored in non-contiguous blocks scattered across a disk, slowing access.
A collection of pre-written, pre-tested routines that programmers can use in their own programs.
A library file that is linked to a program when the program is run, rather than being copied into it when it is compiled.

sections.title: Why a computer needs an operating system
content: System software runs the computer, while application software performs a specific task for the user. The operating system is system software that provides a platform on which programs useful to the user can run. Without it, users would have to control the hardware directly and every application would have to manage memory, files and devices itself. The OS provides a user-system interface: at least a command-line interface and a graphical user interface (GUI). It provides a program-hardware interface, so programmers can write software without knowing how the processor and devices work, and the OS makes the hardware do what the software requires. It also manages resources so that all running processes are served as efficiently as possible.
bullets: It provides an interface between the user and the hardware (CLI and GUI).
It provides a platform on which applications run, so programmers do not need to write hardware-control code.
It manages resources (processor time, memory, storage, devices) between competing processes.
OS tasks can be grouped into those that help the user and those that keep the system running, though some fit both.

sections.title: Process management
content: A process is a program that has begun execution. Many processes run at once and none can run to completion without interruption, so resource management aims for the most efficient use of the system; its two most important parts are scheduling processes and resolving conflicts when two processes need the same resource. The OS allows several processes to share the processor, a technique called multitasking. The scheduler decides which process runs next and gives each one a short time slice, switching between them so quickly that they appear to run at the same time. The OS allocates resources to processes, handles interrupts, and resolves conflicts when two processes need the same resource, so that neither is stuck waiting forever.
bullets: Each process is in a state such as running, ready or blocked (waiting for an event).
Priorities can give more processor time to important tasks.
Detailed scheduling algorithms are covered at A Level in topic 16.1.

sections.title: Memory management
content: Memory management has three aspects. Memory protection ensures that one program cannot use the memory locations allocated to another. The memory organisation scheme is chosen to make the best use of limited memory, for example virtual memory using paging or segmentation, in which part of secondary storage is treated as extra memory and data not currently needed are moved out of RAM. Memory usage optimisation decides which processes should be in main memory at any time and where they are stored. The OS allocates memory to each process when it starts and frees it when it ends.
bullets: Memory protection stops a faulty program crashing other programs or the OS itself.
Memory optimisation decides which data stay in RAM and which can be moved to secondary storage.
Heavy use of virtual memory slows the computer because secondary storage is much slower than RAM.

sections.title: Hardware (input/output and peripheral) management
content: Device management requires installing the appropriate device driver for each device and controlling which processes use it. The OS communicates with input and output devices through device drivers, which translate general OS commands into the specific signals a device understands. It receives and handles interrupts from devices, manages buffers and queues so slow devices do not hold up the processor, and uses spooling so that, for example, several print jobs can be queued on disk and printed in turn.
bullets: New hardware usually needs only a new driver, not a new operating system.
Plug-and-play detects a connected device and loads its driver automatically.
The OS controls which process may use a device at any one time.

sections.title: File management
content: File management provides three main features: file naming conventions, directory (folder) structures and access control mechanisms. The OS organises data on secondary storage into files and directories, keeps track of where each file is physically stored, lets users and programs create, open, save, copy, move, rename and delete files, and controls which users may read or change each file.
bullets: A hierarchical directory structure lets files be organised logically.
File permissions (read, write, execute) are set for users and groups.
The OS hides the physical location of data, so users work with names rather than disk addresses.

sections.title: Security management
content: Security management covers recovery when data are lost, prevention of intrusion, and ensuring data privacy. The OS manages user accounts and authentication with usernames and passwords (or biometrics), assigns access rights so users can only use what they are entitled to, keeps the system updated with security patches, and may include a firewall. It can also log user activity and support backups. Closely related is error detection and recovery: whether an error comes from a badly written program, unsuitable data or a faulty device, the OS must be able to interrupt the running process, give error diagnostics, and in extreme cases shut the system down in an orderly way without losing data.
bullets: Different users can have different privileges, e.g. only an administrator can install software.
Automatic updates close security holes discovered after release.
Encryption of stored data may be provided by the OS.

sections.title: Utility software
content: Utility programs are not part of the normal running of the OS; the user or the OS runs them when needed. A disk formatter removes existing data from a used disk, sets up the file system (a table of contents linking each file to its physical location on the disk, with the disk divided into tracks and sectors), and partitions the disk into logical drives if required. Disk contents analysis and repair software checks the disk for errors. Bad sectors are physical defects, from manufacture or mishandling such as moving a computer carelessly; the utility marks them so the file system no longer uses them. Files damaged by a sudden shutdown or power cut are recovered where possible, otherwise deleted. Defragmentation software deals with a disk that works correctly but slows down: as files are created, extended and deleted they end up split across scattered sectors, so the defragmenter rearranges them so each file occupies a continuous run of sectors, reducing read-write head movement. It needs free working space, so it cannot run on a nearly full disk. A virus checker scans files and memory for malware, comparing them with a database of known virus signatures and watching for suspicious behaviour, then quarantines or deletes infected files; because new viruses appear before the checker is updated, it must be updated regularly and scan all files routinely. File compression software reduces file sizes to save storage and, more importantly, to speed up transmission, for example zipping an email attachment. Back-up software sets a schedule for backups and only creates a new backup when files have changed.
bullets: Defragmenting an SSD is unnecessary, because it has no moving parts, and it wears the flash memory.
A full backup copies everything; an incremental backup copies only changes since the last backup.
Disk analysis tools can also show which files and folders use the most space.

sections.title: Program libraries and DLLs
content: New programs almost always contain errors, so it saves time and trouble to use subroutines from a program library that have already been tried and tested. The most familiar library routines are a language's built-in functions; others are specialist collections, such as libraries of mathematical and statistical procedures. When a program is compiled, the object code must be linked with the code for the library routines it uses. If the routines are linked in before the program is loaded (static linking), every program has its own copy, which makes executable files larger and wastes memory when several processes use the same routine. A dynamic link library (DLL) avoids this: the executable contains only a small piece of code that links to the routine, stored separately, when it is needed during execution, so many processes share one copy.
bullets: Library benefits: saves development time, routines are already tested so they are reliable, and expert code can be used for complex tasks.
DLL benefits: executable files are smaller, one copy in memory can be shared by several programs, and updating the DLL improves every program that uses it without recompiling them.

DLL drawbacks: the program relies on the DLL being present and working; if it is missing, corrupted or a new version contains bugs, the program fails or gives wrong results, and the user will find it hard to work out what is wrong.

comparisonTable.title: Utility software
rows: Sets up the file system and divides the disk into tracks and sectors
A new or reused disk must be prepared before it can store files
Scans for malware and quarantines or deletes it
Protects data from being corrupted, deleted or stolen
Moves the parts of each file on a hard disk so they are stored contiguously
Reduces head movement, so files load faster
Finds and marks bad sectors and recovers data
Prevents data being written to damaged areas
Saves storage and speeds up transmission
Copies files to another medium, often on a schedule
Data can be restored after loss, damage or attack

analysisChains.title: Defragmenting a heavily used hard disk
steps: Over time, files are split into blocks scattered across the disk
Reading a file requires the read/write heads to move to many locations
Defragmentation stores each file's blocks next to each other
The heads move less, so files open faster, and free space becomes one contiguous area
analysisChains.evaluation: Defragmentation helps magnetic hard disks noticeably; it gives no benefit on SSDs and shortens their life, so it should not be used on them.

analysisChains.title: Using a DLL for a spell-checking routine
steps: Several applications link to the same spell-check DLL when they run
Only one copy is stored and loaded into memory
Each application's executable file is smaller
When the DLL is updated with new words, every application benefits without being recompiled
analysisChains.evaluation: Shared DLLs save space and simplify updates, but every application now depends on that file being present and compatible.

analysisChains.title: Scheduling processes with time slices
steps: The processor is given to each ready process in turn for a short time slice
Switching happens many times a second
Users see several programs responding at the same time
But each switch has an overhead, as register contents must be saved and restored
analysisChains.evaluation: Multitasking greatly improves usability and processor use; the scheduler must balance time slice length against switching overhead.

examTips: For each OS management task, give a specific action (e.g. 'allocates memory to processes and prevents them overwriting each other') rather than just naming it.
When a question asks for the need for a utility, explain the problem it solves, not just what it is called.
Separate the benefits of libraries in general from the extra benefits of DLLs.
Say that defragmentation applies to magnetic disks and explain why (fewer head movements).
commonMistakes: Saying the OS is an application program.
Describing defragmentation as deleting files or freeing up space.
Saying formatting only 'cleans' the disk, without mentioning setting up the file system, tracks and sectors.
Claiming antivirus software removes all threats; it only detects threats it recognises or behaviour it flags.
Confusing a DLL with the program itself; the DLL is a separate file loaded at run time.
Listing OS roles without describing what the OS actually does in each.

quickRecall.question: Give two reasons why a computer needs an operating system.
quickRecall.answer: Any two of: provides a user interface, hides hardware complexity, provides a platform for applications, manages resources between programs.

quickRecall.question: What does the OS do in memory management?
quickRecall.answer: Allocates and frees memory for processes, tracks memory use, protects each process's memory, and manages virtual memory.

quickRecall.question: What is a device driver?
quickRecall.answer: Software that translates OS commands into signals a specific hardware device understands.

quickRecall.question: Why is defragmentation useful on a hard disk?
quickRecall.answer: It stores each file contiguously, so the read/write heads move less and files are accessed faster.

quickRecall.question: How does a virus checker detect malware?
quickRecall.answer: It compares files against a database of known virus signatures and monitors for suspicious behaviour.

quickRecall.question: What is a DLL?
quickRecall.answer: A library file linked to a program when it runs, which can be shared by several programs.

quickRecall.question: Give two benefits of using DLLs.
quickRecall.answer: Any two of: smaller executables, one shared copy in memory, updates apply to all programs without recompiling.

quickRecall.question: Give one drawback of DLLs.
quickRecall.answer: The program will not run if the DLL is missing, or an incompatible update can break it.
